newsitem.title: USA: Rubin opposes big tax cuts, says may hurt economy.
newsitem.headline: Rubin opposes big tax cuts, says may hurt economy.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned on Tuesday that big tax cuts could hurt the economy and derail the drive for a balanced budget.
"We must not engage in a 'bidding war' over tax cuts," he said in prepared testimony to the House Budget Committee.
The Clinton administration has proposed what Rubin called a "moderate" tax cut program that would trim revenues by $98.4 billion over five years.

"Tax cuts which are higher would ... run a serious risk of requiring us to make (spending) cuts that unduly harm our economy and our society -- or abandon the goal of a balanced budget, which we absolutely must not do," he said.
Republican lawmakers, who control both houses of Congress, have called for bigger tax cuts than the administration has proposed, including a reduction in the capital gains tax.
In contrast, a coalition of 22 moderate-to-conservative Democrats has argued that taxes should not be cut until the budget is balanced.
The group, known as the "Blue Dog Democrats", has also backed a reduction in annual cost of living increases in such government programs as Social Security.
Rubin said the administration had "policy differences" with the coalition's proposal, but called it "constructive" for the general budget process.
In his prepared testimony, the Treasury chief argued that balancing the budget was critical to the maintenance of a strong U.S. economy over the long term.
"The strong economic conditions we now enjoy are a result of squarely facing our challenges -- in both the private and public sectors," he said.
The result has been more jobs and higher wages. "Average real wages ... now appear to be rising again," Rubin said.
